name: Green Chemistry Principles
what: This subtopic covers the green chemistry principles of catalysis and designing for energy efficiency, and explains how these principles are used to resolve conflicts between optimal reaction rate and maximising yield in equilibrium systems.
why: Green chemistry is an increasingly important part of the VCE study design and reflects the broader shift in chemistry toward sustainable industrial practice. Questions on this topic require students to connect chemical reasoning to environmental and economic considerations.

items.title: I can describe the green chemistry principle of catalysis
items.what: Catalysts increase the rate of a reaction by lowering the activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions. They do not alter the position of equilibrium or the value of K, and they are not consumed in the reaction. Green catalysis favours non-toxic, biodegradable catalysts (such as enzymes) over hazardous chemical catalysts.
items.why: Using catalysts is the primary way to resolve the conflict between low temperature (for high yield) and high rate. Green catalysts also reduce the environmental impact of industrial processes. This principle is directly assessed in VCE.
items.example: In the Haber process, an iron catalyst is used to achieve a commercially acceptable reaction rate at a moderate temperature of around 400-500 degrees C. Without the catalyst, the rate at this temperature would be too slow. The catalyst does not change the equilibrium yield of ammonia.

items.title: I can describe the green chemistry principle of designing for energy efficiency
items.what: Designing for energy efficiency means finding reaction conditions that achieve acceptable yields and rates without requiring excessive energy input. This includes using catalysts to enable lower operating temperatures, optimising reaction pathways to reduce steps, and using heat integration to recover energy.
items.why: Energy consumption is a major environmental and economic consideration in industrial chemistry. Reducing the temperature required for a reaction by using a catalyst directly lowers energy use and reduces greenhouse gas emissions from the process.
items.example: The pharmaceutical synthesis of sertraline (an antidepressant) was redesigned from more than ten reaction steps to three steps using a more selective catalyst and a greener solvent. This reduced energy consumption and waste generation by an order of magnitude.

items.title: I can explain how catalysis and energy efficiency principles resolve conflicts between rate and yield in equilibrium systems
items.what: For an exothermic equilibrium reaction, the conflict is that high temperature improves rate but reduces yield. A catalyst resolves this by enabling acceptable rates at lower temperatures, where yield is higher. This simultaneously satisfies the green chemistry goal of energy efficiency by reducing the temperature needed.
items.why: This is the synthesis question for the entire subtopic and is assessed in VCE extended response. Students must be able to identify the specific conflict in a given reaction and explain precisely how both green chemistry principles address it together.
items.example: In the Haber process, using a high temperature would give fast rates but poor yield of NH3 (exothermic reaction). Using an iron catalyst allows the reaction to proceed at a moderate temperature (around 450 degrees C) with an acceptable rate, achieving better yield while also reducing the energy required to heat the reaction vessel.
